traceSteps.title: Match the mechanism
traceSteps.detail: Ownership, borrowing, `Option`, initialisation checks, bounds checks and `Send`/`Sync` each exclude one of them in safe Rust.

traceSteps.title: Keep the remaining risks
traceSteps.detail: Leaks, deadlocks, panics, overflow policy and logic still need tests and review, as in C.

depth.misconception: “If it compiles in Rust, it is correct.”
depth.correction: If it compiles without `unsafe`, it has no undefined behaviour. It can still leak, deadlock, panic or compute the wrong result; the compiler removes a class of bugs, not the need for tests.
depth.transferChallenge: Write a safe Rust program that deadlocks with two `Mutex`es locked in opposite orders by two threads, then fix it with one global lock order.

title: What Safe Rust Rules Out

writing.summary: Safe Rust rules out the memory and thread bugs that are undefined behaviour in C, but not leaks, deadlocks, panics or wrong logic.
writing.rule: Safe Rust has no undefined behaviour: use after free, double free, dangling references, out-of-bounds access, null dereference, uninitialised reads and data races are rejected or checked; leaks, deadlocks, panics, logic errors and wrapping arithmetic in release builds are not.
writing.explanation:
In C, executing an undefined operation makes the whole program meaningless, and the optimiser is allowed to assume it never happens. The example's four cases compile without a single warning under `-Wall -Wextra`; each one fails only when it runs, and only a sanitizer build says why: `stack-buffer-overflow`, `heap-use-after-free`, a load of a null pointer and `attempting double-free`.

Safe Rust closes each of these by construction. Ownership means one owner frees each value once, so double free and use after free cannot be written. Borrow checking means a reference cannot outlive its value or overlap a writer. References are never null; absence is `Option`. A binding must be initialised on every path before it is read, or the program is rejected with `E0381`. `Send` and `Sync`, together with borrowing, make data races a compile error. Indexing is the one run-time check: `xs[i]` with a bad index panics, and `xs.get(i)` returns `None`, so an out-of-bounds read never touches the neighbouring memory.

"Safe" means free of undefined behaviour, not correct. Safe Rust can still leak memory (`Box::leak`, `mem::forget` and `Rc` cycles are all safe), deadlock on two `Mutex`es taken in different orders, compute the wrong answer, run out of memory or stack, and panic. A panic is defined behaviour: the thread unwinds and runs destructors, or the process aborts if it is configured to. Integer overflow is defined too, but in release builds it wraps unless you choose `checked_` or keep `overflow-checks` on.

`unsafe` re-enables specific powers that safe code lacks: dereferencing raw pointers, calling `unsafe` functions including every C function, accessing mutable statics, implementing `unsafe` traits and reading `union` fields. Inside those blocks every C undefined behaviour is possible again, and the guarantee for the whole program rests on each `unsafe` block being right. That is why such blocks are kept small and documented; a later lesson shows how.
writing.exampleCaption: A checked index, a move instead of a second owner, `Option` instead of null, explicit wrapping, and a leak that is wasteful but safe.
writing.task: Run the C program's cases under a sanitizer in your head, match each one to the Rust rule that excludes it, then decide what the practice program needs before it compiles.
writing.success: You can name the Rust mechanism behind each excluded C bug, and list three kinds of bug safe Rust still allows.
writing.question: Which of these can a program written entirely in safe Rust still do?
answers: Read a freed heap buffer through a stale reference
Index one element past the end of an array without being stopped
Leak memory with `Box::leak` or deadlock on two `Mutex`es
writing.feedback: Leaks and deadlocks are bugs, not undefined behaviour, so safe Rust allows them. The other three are rejected at compile time or stopped by a bounds-check panic.

recall.question: Is a panic in Rust undefined behaviour, like an out-of-bounds read in C?
recall.answer: No. A panic is defined: by default the thread unwinds, runs destructors and reports the message, and with `panic = "abort"` the process stops immediately. A bad index in safe Rust becomes this defined panic instead of a read of neighbouring memory.

recall.question: Does this compile, and is it safe?
recall.answer: Yes and yes: it prints `done`. Leaking is not undefined behaviour, so `mem::forget`, `Box::leak` and `Rc` cycles are all safe. The memory is never returned to the allocator, which wastes it but cannot corrupt anything.

bridge.fromCaption: Four undefined behaviours that compile without a warning; sanitizers report a stack overflow, a use after free, a null load and a double free.

contrasts.from: Use after free, double free and dangling pointers compile and are undefined.
contrasts.rust: Ownership and borrow checking reject them at compile time.

contrasts.from: Out-of-bounds reads and NULL dereferences are undefined.
contrasts.rust: Indexing is bounds-checked (a defined panic); absence is `Option`, never a null reference.

contrasts.from: Reading an uninitialised variable is at most a warning.
contrasts.rust: Every binding must be initialised on every path before it is read (`E0381`).

contrasts.from: Leaks, deadlocks and logic errors are the programmer's problem.
contrasts.rust: They still are: safe Rust excludes undefined behaviour, not bugs.
